entry.title: literature review of recurrent depth latent reasoning

link.title: literature review of recurrent depth latent reasoning

entry.content:
The authors’ path

The first and last authors of Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach are Jonas Geiping and Tom Goldstein. Their previous research provides two particularly relevant foundations for this paper: making language models more computationally efficient, and enabling neural networks to solve harder problems by performing more computation.

Jonas Geiping: Making language models more efficient

Jonas Geiping is a researcher at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems. His research focuses on the efficiency, safety, and reliability of modern machine learning systems, particularly large language models.

One of his most relevant earlier works is Cramming: Training a Language Model on a Single GPU in One Day (ICML 2023), co-authored with Tom Goldstein.

Rather than asking how much performance could be gained by increasing computational resources, they explored how much could be achieved under strict computational constraints. By optimizing the training pipeline, they demonstrated that a BERT-like language model could achieve competitive performance after just 24 hours of training on a single GPU.

The connection to the current paper is clear: both studies challenge the assumption that improving language models necessarily requires increasing their parameter count. While Cramming investigated how to use a limited training budget efficiently, the recurrent-depth paper explores how to use additional computation at inference time without increasing the number of model parameters.

Tom Goldstein: From optimization to recurrent reasoning

Tom Goldstein is a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Maryland and Director of the Maryland Center for Machine Learning. His research combines optimization, machine learning, and efficient computing.

The recurrent-depth paper builds especially closely on his earlier research into what his group calls “deep thinking” networks.

In The Uncanny Similarity of Recurrence and Depth (2021), Goldstein and his collaborators showed that recurrent neural networks could reproduce some of the benefits of deeper feedforward networks by repeatedly applying the same layers.

This idea was extended in Can You Learn an Algorithm? Generalizing from Easy to Hard Problems with Recurrent Networks (NeurIPS 2021). The researchers demonstrated that recurrent networks trained on relatively simple reasoning problems, such as small mazes, could generalize to harder instances by performing additional iterations at inference time.

These results established a central motivation for the current paper: a model’s computational depth does not have to be fixed at training time. Instead, the model can reuse learned operations for as long as a problem requires.

How their research connects to this paper

The recurrent-depth paper can be viewed as a convergence of these two research directions:

  • From Geiping and Goldstein’s Cramming: Efficient model design and careful use of computational resources can provide alternatives to simply increasing model size.
  • From Goldstein’s earlier deep-thinking research: Recurrent computation enables models to increase their effective depth and potentially solve harder problems without introducing additional parameters.

The current work combines these ideas at the scale of modern language modeling. The authors train a 3.5-billion-parameter Transformer with a recurrent block that can be executed repeatedly at inference time, allowing the model to perform additional reasoning internally rather than generating longer chains of thought.

The important progression is from demonstrating recurrence on relatively controlled reasoning tasks to testing whether the same principle can work in a large-scale, pretrained language model.

This makes the paper more than an isolated architectural experiment. It represents a continuation of the authors’ broader investigation into how neural networks can use computation more effectively, both during training and at inference time.

The bigger picture

The authors’ research trajectory suggests an alternative perspective on scaling language models. Instead of treating parameter count and training data as the primary ways to improve performance, their work investigates whether the organization and allocation of computation can be equally important.

The recurrent-depth paper is an important step in this direction, although it leaves open whether latent recurrence can match the reasoning capabilities and efficiency of leading models that rely on explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning.

The main takeaway: This paper connects two established research threads from its authors: efficient language-model training and recurrent neural computation. Its novelty lies in bringing these ideas together to demonstrate test-time reasoning through increased depth rather than increased token generation.
entry.summary: How Jonas Geiping and Tom Goldstein's earlier work on efficient language models and recurrent computation converged in a new approach to test-time scaling.

entry.title: Before you read MSAR: the three ideas it builds on

link.title: Before you read MSAR: the three ideas it builds on

entry.content:
Our reading group spent this week on “Multi-Stream Attention Residuals” (Qin et al., 2026), which proposes a new way to connect the layers of a Transformer and reports solid gains on 18B and 28B parameter models.

The paper builds on three earlier ideas and assumes you already know them. This post walks through those ideas in order, with the problem each one leaves open, and shows how the last of those problems leads directly to MSAR. If the background is familiar, skip to the final section.

The question

A token passes through the layers of a Transformer one by one, and each layer changes it a little. So every architecture has to decide: how does a layer draw on the layers below it? The three ideas below are three answers.

Answer 1 · Residual connections: add everything

This is the standard connection. Each layer adds its output to a running sum, and the next layer reads that sum. It is simple and stable, and it works. The cost is that every output lands in the same vector with the same weight. As the network gets deeper, the contribution of early layers is diluted, and nothing downstream can recover it on its own.

Answer 2 · Hyper-Connections: several streams in parallel

Hyper-Connections replace the single residual stream with several streams that run through the whole network, mixed at every layer by learned matrices. Information no longer has to collapse into one sum. mHC from DeepSeek, which the paper refers to often, is a variant that constrains the mixing matrices to keep training stable.

The limitation is that the mixing is learned once and then frozen. Every token, on every input, gets the same mix. But which layer holds the useful information varies from token to token: for one token it is layer 2, for the next it is layer 7. A fixed mix cannot track that. Running several streams also multiplies memory.

Answer 3 · Attention Residuals: let the input decide

Attention Residuals replace the sum with attention over the outputs of the earlier layers. It is the familiar mechanism, applied along the depth axis rather than the sequence axis. The twist is that there are no Q, K or V projections. Each layer has a single learned query vector, and those earlier outputs serve as both keys and values. The method adds almost no parameters, yet the weights now depend on the input: one token can draw mostly on layer 2 while its neighbour draws on layer 7.

The three answers. Arrow width shows how much the top layer takes from each earlier layer. Only in the third case does the pattern change from token to token.

The problem that remains: a single head

Attention over the sequence uses several heads, each with its own view of the sentence. What makes them different is either separate projection matrices or separate slices of the vector. Attention Residuals has neither option: there are no matrices, and slicing the vector degrades the selection. Run four heads and they all see the same outputs, so they end up nearly identical. This is the point where MSAR begins.

What MSAR adds

MSAR gives each head a different view without adding matrices or slicing the vector. Before a head selects among layers, each output is passed through a causal convolution along the sequence, blending in a few of the preceding tokens, and each head uses a different window size. The four heads therefore see four slightly different views of the same column and make different selections. How the heads are fused, and why this costs no extra memory, is covered in the method section, which reads easily once this background is in place.

Left: four heads without the convolution see identical inputs. Right: each head gets its own window, and so its own selection.

One reading tip: the paper calls this a “depth-wise” convolution, but it runs over tokens, not over layers. The attention is along depth; the convolution is along the sequence.

In short

There are three ways to connect layers, and what separates them is whether the weights are fixed or computed from the input. Attention Residuals is the dynamic one, but without projection matrices it is limited to a single head. MSAR gives each head a different window over the sequence, and that is the whole idea. With these three pieces in place, the paper is a straightforward read.

Posted at: LinkedIn · X
entry.summary: A short guide to the background the paper assumes: residual connections, Hyper-Connections and Attention Residuals, and the problem that leads to MSAR.

entry.title: Copyediting Section 7 of Recurrent Depth
entry.content:
What I changed and why

Section 7 is intriguing because it is where the paper looks directly at what the recurrence does to a token’s latent state as the model iterates. With that being said, the section does not separate what the authors observed from what they infer, and several claims extend beyond the figures: the title attributes the patterns to scale although no smaller model is shown, and the text and captions disagree on how widely orbits occur and what sliders are for. I introduced the three patterns up front, stated the evidence base once, moved the interpretations to a closing paragraph and removed claims the figures do not support, reducing the section from 568 to under 400 words.

Before and after

Before

Finally, what is the model doing while recurring in latent space? To understand this question better, we analyze the trajectories { 𝐬 i } i = 1 r of the model on a few qualitative examples. We are especially interested in understanding what patterns emerge, simply by training this model at scale. In comparison to previous work, such as Bai et al. (2019), where the training objective directly encodes a prior that pushes trajectories to a fixed point, we only train with our truncated unrolling objective.

Figure 11 shows the norm distance ‖ 𝐬 i − 𝐬 ∗ ‖ between each 𝐬 i in a trajectory and an approximate limit point 𝐬 ∗ computed with 128 iterations. We show the sentence top to bottom and iterations from left to right. We clearly see that convergence behavior depends on context. We see that key parts of the question, and the start of the model response, are “deliberated” much more in latent space. The context dependence can also be seen in the different behavior among the three identical tokens representing each of the three dots. Also note that the distance to 𝐬 ∗ does not always decrease monotonically (e.g. for school); the model may also trace out complicated orbits in its latent trajectory while processing information, even though this is not represented explicitly in our training objective.

We look at trajectories for select tokens in more detail in Figure 12. We compute a PCA decomposition of latent trajectories over all tokens in a sequence, and then show several individual trajectories projected onto the first six PCA directions. See the appendix for more examples. Many tokens simply converge to a fixed point, such as the token in the top row. Yet, for harder questions, such as in the 2nd row5, the state of the token quickly falls into an orbit pattern in all three pairs of PCA directions. The use of multi-dimensional orbits like these could serve a similar purpose to periodic patterns sometimes observed in fixed-depth transformers trained for arithmetic tasks (Nanda et al., 2022), but we find these patterns extend far beyond arithmetic for our model. We often also observe the use of orbits on tokens such as “makes” (see Figure 16) or “thinks” that determine the structure of the response.

Aside from orbits, we also observe the model encoding particular key tokens as “sliders”, as seen in the middle of the bottom row in Figure 12 (which is the token “wrong”, from the same message as already shown in Figure 11). In these motions the trajectory noticeably drifts in a single direction, which the model could use to implement a mechanism to count how many iterations have occurred.

The emergence of structured trajectories in latent space gives us a glimpse into how the model performs its computations. Unlike the discrete sequential chain of reasoning seen in verbalized chain-of-thought approaches, we observe rich geometric patterns including orbits, convergent paths, and drifts - means to organize its computational process spatially. This suggests the model is independently learning to leverage the high-dimensional nature of its latent space to implement reasoning in new ways.

Path Independence. We verify that our models maintain path independence, in the sense of Anil et al. (2022), despite their complex, learned dynamics, which we discussed prior (see also the additional examples in Appendix Figure 22). When re-initializing from multiple starting states 𝐬 0 , the model moves in similar trajectories, exhibiting consistent behavior. The same orbital patterns, fixed points, or directional drifts emerge regardless of initialization.

After

What Patterns Emerge in Latent Space

What does the model compute while it iterates in latent space? We examine the trajectories \(\{\mathbf{s}_i\}_{i=1}^{r}\) of every token in a small set of hand-picked prompts, so the analysis in this section is qualitative. Unlike deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019), our training objective does not pull the state toward a fixed point, so any structure in these trajectories is learned by the model rather than imposed by the objective.

In these examples, each token’s state follows one of three patterns. Figure 12 shows selected trajectories projected onto the leading PCA directions of the prompt. Many tokens converge to a fixed point. Others enter an orbit and keep circling instead of converging. We observe orbits on numbers in math problems, such as the “3” in a GSM8k question about a three-egg omelette (see also Figure 16), and on some tokens that shape the response, such as “makes” and “thinks”, but not on trivia questions. A third group, which we call sliders, drifts steadily in one direction, for example the token “wrong” in an unsafe prompt.

Convergence speed depends on context, not only on the token itself. Figure 11 plots each token’s distance to \(\mathbf{s}^*\), its state after 128 iterations. The key words of the question and the first tokens of the response converge most slowly, and three identical dot tokens in the same prompt behave differently. For some tokens, such as “school”, the distance oscillates rather than decreasing monotonically.

These patterns do not depend on the initial state. Restarting the iteration from different random states \(\mathbf{s}_0\) yields the same fixed point, orbit or slide for each token (Appendix Figure 22), consistent with the path independence (Anil et al., 2022) that the random initialization is designed to promote (Section 3.1).

The function of these patterns remains speculative. Orbits on numbers may serve a role similar to the periodic representations found in transformers trained on arithmetic (Nanda et al., 2022). Sliders could act as a counter of elapsed iterations, or hold a concept the model is still processing. A handful of examples cannot distinguish between these possibilities, and we do not test either hypothesis here.

The general rule

Separate observation from interpretation. Report what the evidence shows first, and present any interpretation afterwards, explicitly marked as a hypothesis. A useful check is that deleting every interpretive sentence should still leave a complete and accurate description of the results.
entry.summary: Section 7 interleaves observation and speculation about the model's latent trajectories; this edit separates the two.

entry.title: A Scalable Recurrent Architecture - Rewritten for Easier Understanding

link.title: A Scalable Recurrent Architecture - Rewritten for Easier Understanding

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The main problem I had with the original text was that it had many equations without an in-depth explanation of each. Making it the readers responsibility to cross-reference with the figure.

As for the structure of the text, I personally would prefer having the motivation prior to the actual architecture. This helps understanding the reasons for such architecture choices and creates a more natural reading flow. Furthermore I try to include subtitles and lists whenever is possible to avoid large text blobs.

Before and after

Before

3.1. Macroscopic Design

The model is primarily structured around decoder-only transformer blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017; Radford et al., 2019). However these blocks are structured into three functional groups, the prelude \(P\), which embeds the input data into a latent space using multiple transformer layers, then the core recurrent block \(R\), which is the central unit of recurrent computation modifying states \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times h}\), and finally the coda \(C\), which un-embeds from latent space using several layers and also contains the prediction head of the model. The core block is set between the prelude and coda blocks, and by looping the core we can put an indefinite amount of verses in our song.

Given a number of recurrent iterations \(r\), and a sequence of input tokens \(\mathbf{x} \in V^{n}\) these groups are used in the following way to produce output probabilities \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times |V|}\)

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{e} &= P(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{s}_0 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_{n \cdot h}) \\ \mathbf{s}_i &= R(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{s}_{i-1}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, \dots, r\} \\ \mathbf{p} &= C(\mathbf{s}_r) \end{aligned} \]

where \(\sigma\) is some standard deviation for initializing the random state. This process is shown in Figure 2. Given an initial random state \(\mathbf{s}_0\), the model repeatedly applies the core block \(R\), which accepts the latent state \(\mathbf{s}_{i-1}\) and the embedded input \(\mathbf{e}\) and outputs a new latent state \(\mathbf{s}_i\). After finishing all iterations, the coda block processes the last state and produces the probabilities of the next token.

This architecture is based on deep thinking literature, where it is shown that injecting the latent inputs \(\mathbf{e}\) in every step (Bansal et al., 2022) and initializing the latent vector with a random state stabilizes the recurrence and promotes convergence to a steady state independent of initialization, i.e. path independence (Anil et al., 2022).

Motivation for this Design. This recurrent design is the minimal setup required to learn stable iterative operators. A good example is gradient descent of a function \(E(x, y)\), where \(x\) may be the variable of interest and \(y\) the data. Gradient descent on this function starts from an initial random state, here \(x_0\), and repeatedly applies a simple operation (the gradient of the function it optimizes), that depends on the previous state \(x_k\) and data \(y\). Note that we need to use \(y\) in every step to actually optimize our function. Similarly we repeatedly inject the data \(\mathbf{e}\) in our set-up in every step of the recurrence. If \(\mathbf{e}\) was provided only at the start, e.g. via \(\mathbf{s}_0 = \mathbf{e}\), then the iterative process would not be stable1, as its solution would depend only on its boundary conditions.

The structure of using several layers to embed input tokens into a hidden latent space is based on empirical results analyzing standard fixed-depth transformers (Skean et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Kaplan et al., 2024). This body of research shows that the initial and the end layers of LLMs are noticeably different, whereas middle layers are interchangeable and permutable. For example, Kaplan et al. (2024) show that within a few layers standard models already embed sub-word tokens into single concepts in latent space, on which the model then operates.

After

3.1. Macroscopic Design

The model suggests 3 new functional groups: prelude \(P\), the core recurrent block \(R\), and coda \(C\). While keeping the stucture primarily around decoder-only transformer blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017; Radford et al., 2019).

The idea behind the 3 groups.

  • \(P\), the prelude, embeds the input data into a latent space using multiple transformer layers.
  • \(R\), the core recurrent block, is the central unit. It's responsible for recurrent computation modifying states \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times h}\).
  • \(C\), the coda, has 2 main responsibilities. It un-embeds from latent space using several layers and contains the prediction head of the model.
Similarly to a song, the core block is set between the prelude and coda blocks. And by looping the core we can put an indefinite amount of verses.

Motivation for this Design.

The minimal setup required for learn stable iterative operators includes the following.

  • An initial starting state (a random starting point, \(s_0\)).
  • A previous state to build upon (\(s_{i-1}\)).
  • The input data (\(e\)) injected at every single step.
A good example is gradient descent of a function \(E(x, y)\), where \(x\) may be the variable of interest and \(y\) the data. Gradient descent on this function starts from an initial random state, here \(x_0\), and repeatedly applies a simple operation (the gradient of the function it optimizes), that depends on the previous state \(x_k\) and data \(y\). Note that we need to use \(y\) in every step to actually optimize our function.

The formal architecture.

Given a number of recurrent iterations \(r\), and a sequence of input tokens \(\mathbf{x} \in V^{n}\) these groups are used in the following way to produce output probabilities \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times |V|}\). As shown in Figure 2.

  • The prelude produces the embedded input data \(\mathbf{e} = P(\mathbf{x})\).
  • The initial random state \(s_0\) is drawn from some standard deviation \(\sigma\) distributed normally. \(\mathbf{s}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_{n \cdot h})\)
  • The core recurrent block repeatedly produces a new state \(s_i\) while still using the original embedded input data \(\mathbf{e}\). \(\mathbf{s}_i = R(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{s}_{i-1}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, \dots, r\}\).
  • The coda produces the final output probabilities for predicting the next token from the last state. \(\mathbf{p} = C(\mathbf{s}_r)\).

Notice we repeatedly inject the data \(\mathbf{e}\) in our set-up in every step of the recurrence. Similarly to what's mentioned in the motivation. If \(\mathbf{e}\) was provided only at the start, e.g. via \(\mathbf{s}_0 = \mathbf{e}\), then the iterative process would not be stable1, as its solution would depend only on its boundary conditions.

This architecture is based on deep thinking literature, where it is shown that injecting the latent inputs \(\mathbf{e}\) in every step (Bansal et al., 2022) and initializing the latent vector with a random state stabilizes the recurrence and promotes convergence to a steady state independent of initialization, i.e. path independence (Anil et al., 2022).

The inspiration for the architecture.

The structure of using several layers to embed input tokens into a hidden latent space is based on empirical results analyzing standard fixed-depth transformers (Skean et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Kaplan et al., 2024). This body of research shows that the initial and the end layers of LLMs are noticeably different, whereas middle layers are interchangeable and permutable. For example, Kaplan et al. (2024) show that within a few layers standard models already embed sub-word tokens into single concepts in latent space, on which the model then operates.

The general rule

The general rules I used in my writing were “known before new” (mention known concepts before introducing new ones), “anchor the reader before adding weight” (establish the main concept immediately, such as in the initial sentence or title), and “one core claim per paragraph”.
entry.summary: Rewriting the section 3.1 explaining the macro of the latent recurrent-depth model.

entry.title: Copyediting the Introduction of Recurrent Depth

link.title: Copyediting the Introduction of Recurrent Depth

entry.content:
What I changed and why

Although the introduction acknowledges that recurrent computation is an established idea, it does not clearly distinguish earlier work from this paper’s contribution, leaving the detailed comparison until Section 8. I rewrote Section 1 to introduce the closest prior work before explaining what this paper adds: a concrete architecture and training procedure, a demonstration at scale, and measured improvements from additional inference-time computation. This makes the paper’s contribution clearer before readers reach the methods and results.

Before and after

Before

Humans naturally expend more mental effort solving some problems than others. While humans are capable of thinking over long time spans by verbalizing intermediate results and writing them down, a substantial amount of thought happens through complex, recurrent firing patterns in the brain, before the first word of an answer is uttered.

Early attempts at increasing the power of language models focused on scaling model size, a practice that requires extreme amounts of data and computation. More recently, researchers have explored ways to enhance the reasoning capability of models by scaling test time computation. The mainstream approach involves post-training on long chain-of-thought examples to develop the model’s ability to verbalize intermediate calculations in its context window and thereby externalize thoughts.

However, the constraint that expensive internal reasoning must always be projected down to a single verbalized next token appears wasteful; it is plausible that models could be more competent if they were able to natively “think” in their continuous latent space. One way to unlock this untapped dimension of additional compute involves adding a recurrent unit to a model. This unit runs in a loop, iteratively processing and updating its hidden state and enabling computations to be carried on indefinitely. While this is not currently the dominant paradigm, this idea is foundational to machine learning and has been (re-)discovered in every decade, for example as recurrent neural networks, diffusion models, and as universal or looped transformers.

In this work, we show that depth-recurrent language models can learn effectively, be trained in an efficient manner, and demonstrate significant performance improvements under the scaling of test-time compute. Our proposed transformer architecture is built upon a latent depth-recurrent block that is run for a randomly sampled number of iterations during training. We show that this paradigm can scale to several billion parameters and over half a trillion tokens of pretraining data. At test-time, the model can improve its performance through recurrent reasoning in latent space, enabling it to compete with other open-source models that benefit from more parameters and training data. Additionally, we show that recurrent depth models naturally support a number of features at inference time that require substantial tuning and research effort in non-recurrent models, such as per-token adaptive compute, (self)-speculative decoding, and KV-cache sharing. We finish out our study by tracking token trajectories in latent space, showing that a number of interesting computation behaviors simply emerge with scale, such as the model rotating shapes in latent space for numerical computations.

On a more philosophical note, we hope that latent reasoning captures facets of human reasoning that defy verbalization, such as spatial thinking, physical intuition or (motor) planning. Over many iterations of the recurrent process, reasoning in a high-dimensional vector space would enable the deep exploration of multiple directions simultaneously, instead of linear thinking, leading to a system capable of exhibiting novel and complex reasoning behavior.

Scaling compute in this manner is not at odds with scaling through extended (verbalized) inference scaling (Shao et al., 2024), or scaling parameter counts in pretraining (Kaplan et al., 2020), we argue it may build a third axis on which to scale model performance.

After

Language models can allocate additional computation to difficult problems by generating intermediate reasoning tokens, as in chain-of-thought approaches. An alternative is to perform additional computation directly in the model’s continuous latent space before predicting the next token. We investigate this approach through recurrent depth, in which a shared block of transformer layers is applied repeatedly to update a hidden state. This allows the model to increase its effective computational depth at inference time without increasing its number of parameters or generating additional intermediate tokens.

Prior work. Recurrent computation across transformer depth has been studied extensively. Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019) applied recurrence across transformer layers, while ALBERT (Lan et al., 2019) demonstrated parameter sharing across layers at scale, using a fixed number of layer applications. Subsequent work on “deep thinking” networks showed that randomized iteration counts and repeated input injection can enable learned algorithms to generalize to additional computation at inference time (Schwarzschild et al., 2021b; Bansal et al., 2022). Our architecture and training procedure build on these findings. Related studies have further investigated the theoretical properties and learning capabilities of looped transformers, primarily through theoretical and small-scale analyses (Giannou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a; Fan et al., 2025).

Deep equilibrium models provide another perspective on iterative computation, using fixed-point formulations (Bai et al., 2019). In contrast, our training procedure explicitly unrolls a sampled number of recurrent iterations and truncates backpropagation through the recurrent block to the final steps. As we show in Section 7, the resulting latent trajectories exhibit a range of behaviors beyond simple convergence to fixed points.

Recent work has also explored latent reasoning by adapting pretrained language models. For example, Hao et al. (2024) train a pretrained transformer to reuse its final hidden state as an input, using reasoning chains to learn continuous intermediate computation. Our approach instead incorporates recurrence directly into the architecture during pretraining and optimizes a standard next-token prediction objective with variable recurrent depth. Unlike approaches that use reasoning chains to supervise latent computation, our method does not require a separate training curriculum for intermediate reasoning steps. However, our pretraining mixture does include instruction and mathematical reasoning data, as detailed in Section 4.1 and Appendix C.

Our contribution. Building on these earlier approaches, we investigate whether recurrent-depth language models can be trained at substantial scale and effectively exploit additional computation at inference time. Our contribution is not the introduction of recurrence itself, but rather a scalable architecture and training procedure, together with an empirical evaluation of their behavior and inference-time capabilities.

Our architecture consists of an input-processing prelude, a shared recurrent core, and an output-processing coda. At each iteration, the recurrent core updates the latent state while receiving the prelude’s representation of the input. During training, we sample recurrence counts from a heavy-tailed distribution and backpropagate through at most the final eight recurrent iterations, reducing activation memory requirements (Section 3). We also identify normalization and initialization choices that are necessary for stable training at scale. In unsuccessful training runs, the model either collapsed its token representations or learned to ignore the recurrent state, preventing effective use of additional iterations (Section 4.3).

Our main contributions are threefold:

  1. Training at scale. We train a 3.5B-parameter recurrent language model on approximately 800B tokens and release the training code, data, and model checkpoints. Our results demonstrate that variable-depth recurrence can be trained successfully at substantial language-model scale, extending earlier small-scale studies of looped transformers (Sections 3–4).
  2. Scaling test-time computation. We evaluate the same model at different recurrence counts and show that additional iterations improve performance, with saturation depending on the task. Mathematical reasoning and coding tasks generally benefit from more iterations than tasks such as HellaSwag (Section 5). The model can operate at inference compute budgets comparable to those of fixed-depth models with approximately 50B parameters. We also compare against a non-recurrent baseline trained with the same data and training setup for 180B tokens. Although recurrence provides substantial improvements on harder tasks, the comparison is not FLOP-matched, since additional iterations increase computation.
  3. Inference capabilities and latent-state analysis. We demonstrate per-token adaptive stopping and KV-cache sharing without additional training, and describe how recurrence can support continuous state reuse and self-speculative decoding (Section 6). We further analyze latent-state trajectories and identify several recurring patterns, including convergence, orbits, and directional drifts, providing insight into the model’s iterative computation (Section 7).

Our results establish the feasibility of training recurrent-depth language models at scale and improving their performance through additional latent computation. Nevertheless, the model remains a proof of concept based on a single successful large-scale training run. Its relatively small parameter count should not be interpreted as an equivalent reduction in computational cost, since repeated application of the recurrent core increases the required FLOPs. Further work is needed to establish how recurrent depth compares with alternative approaches under matched compute budgets. We view recurrent depth as a complementary direction to parameter scaling and explicit chain-of-thought reasoning, offering an additional axis along which language-model computation can be scaled.

The general rule

Present the relevant related work before stating the paper’s contribution. Make clear which ideas come from earlier work and credit their authors, so readers can identify what the paper adds without mistaking inherited ideas for new inventions.
entry.summary: What is actually new about recurrent reasoning? Making the paper's contribution clear from the start.

entry.title: Can we read Huginn’s latent thoughts? It depends on the lens

link.title: Can we read Huginn’s latent thoughts? It depends on the lens

entry.content:
This week’s paper claims that looping a recurrent block is a form of reasoning in latent space. If that is true, we should be able to watch the answer form across the recurrences. Two papers tried to do this on Huginn, the model from this week’s paper.

Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer (Lu, Yang, Lee, Li & Liu, 2025): Decodes Huginn’s intermediate states with the logit lens and with a coda lens, which runs the state through Huginn’s own two learned decoder blocks. The two lenses disagree about which recurrent blocks are readable, and neither shows a clear latent chain of thought.

Looped Transformers under the Jacobian Lens: Does the Global Workspace Survive Recurrence? (anonymous ICLR 2027 submission, under review): Fits a lens aimed at each stage of the loop and finds the answer is readable at every recurrence. Each lens can only read about two recurrences ahead, though, so a lens that fails on early states says nothing about whether those states contain the answer. (Caveat - still under review. This looks good and highly relevant, but we should probably wait for a peer-reviewed version)

Why the two papers seem to disagree

The Jacobian lens is a linear map: the average, over many prompts, of how a change in one hidden state moves a later one. A logit-lens or coda-lens readout asks the early state to look like the final one. The Jacobian lens instead learns how to carry the early state forward to a chosen target recurrence (4, 8, 12 or 16) and reads it there.

On “The capital city of the country famous for sushi is”, Tokyo ranks first at recurrences 2–3 through the lens aimed at recurrence 4. Through the lenses aimed at 8, 12 and 16 it ranks first at recurrences 7, 10–11 and 14–15. The same forward pass looks empty or full depending on which lens you use and how far it has to reach. That is one explanation for the disagreement Lu et al. saw.

Here a recurrence is one pass of Huginn’s 4-layer core, so “two recurrences” is about 8 transformer layers.

What the model seems to be doing

  • It recomputes rather than remembers. Shrinking the input that Huginn re-injects at every recurrence to a quarter of its size breaks the answer on every tested prompt. Swapping in another prompt’s input changes the answer within about two recurrences.
  • It can steer old content but can’t report new content. If you swap a concept the model already computed, it reports the new one 98% of the time (124/126). If you inject a concept it never computed, it never names it (0/97). Ouro, a looped model trained to be readable after every loop, manages 31%.
  • Only late edits stick. Edits in the last lens window are as effective as edits everywhere (25/192 flips each). Edits in the window before it get 5/192.

Questions for class

  • If the answer is readable from recurrence 2–3, what are the remaining recurrences doing? Is that “reasoning”, or re-deriving the same answer from the input?
  • The paper’s convergent, orbiting and drifting trajectories (Figure 12): does “the state keeps being rebuilt from the input” change how we read them?
  • How much of what we call latent reasoning is a property of the model, and how much of the instrument we use to look?

Bonus, if you care about compute: What Does Another Loop Buy? (anonymous ICLR 2027 submission) stops looping once the attention pattern stops changing between iterations. On Huginn it saves 48% of the compute for a 2-point drop on GSM8K, and beats a KL-based exit at matched compute. That is a simple alternative to the early-exit criterion in this week’s paper.
entry.summary: Two papers that try to decode the recurrent states of this week's model, and why they seem to disagree.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
Papers worth knowing this week

  • Latent Recurrent Thoughts: Recurrent Refinement of Proposed Latents for Reasoning with Frozen LLMs (Chen & Fu, September 2026): Introduces a lightweight, task-specific recurrent network that iteratively refines continuous reasoning representations while keeping the underlying LLM frozen. The approach improves reasoning on symbolic and natural-language tasks by training only a small fraction of the model’s parameters, without requiring explicit reasoning traces for symbolic tasks.

  • Latent Reasoning with Supervised Thinking States (Amos et al., February 2026): Proposes generating intermediate natural-language thoughts, compressing them into continuous hidden states, and feeding them into subsequent computations without extending the LLM’s context. By supervising these thoughts using Chain-of-Thought examples, the method enables efficient parallel training and faster inference while retaining much of the reasoning accuracy of explicit CoT.

entry.title: Visualizing a core idea
entry.content:
Throughout the paper, the authors frame depth recurrence as a mechanism for implicit latent reasoning. Computational depth should then reflect the complexity of the required reasoning, rather than improving accuracy.

This is reflected in their design choices:

  • Training data - composed of relatively heavy reasoning domains.
  • Training mechanisms - randomizing the depth, decoupling it from the direct accuracy metrics.

Here I visualize 3 points from the paper emphasizing the depth as a reasoning mechanism:

1. “the recurrent model outperforms its baseline with an especially pronounced advantage on harder tasks”

(5.3 Where does recurrence help most?)

Figure 7 shows that tasks that require more reasoning take more iterations to saturate the performance. Tables 1 and 4 include similar relevant evaluations that can be visualised in a similar plot:

Blue shades are simple tasks, and green shades are tasks requiring more reasoning. Reading the text, I was expecting the trends to show a later convergence for reasoning demanding tasks than the simple ones, but this is not as convincing.

2. “when more context is given, the model can reason about more information in context,…, mirroring generalization improvements shown for recurrence”

(Recurrence and Context)

In Figure 9 they show that as the model gets more shots (examples of the task), the accuracy saturates later, maybe indicating the model uses the examples as part of a complex reasoning. Table 4 compares closed book to open book tasks, in a similar context of open book allowing the preference reasoning over memorization.

Score shows performance (%). The model improves in an open-book scenario, showing similar improvement to other open source models.

3. “…the model exiting earlier on high school mathematics, but taking on average 3.5 steps more on moral scenarios”

(6.1. Zero-Shot Adaptive Compute at Test-Time)

Using the model for adaptive compute, they use a convergence metric to allow early exit. The idea is that simpler tasks, that require less reasoning, should converge and exit earlier. Figure 10 shows the distribution of steps to exit on different tasks, where simple tasks like high school math exit earlier than heavy reasoning tasks like moral scenarios.

Focusing on the peak of the density functions, it’s simpler to see that Continuous Chain-of-Thought (6.3) has little contribution, but the effect of the task domain is clear.
entry.summary: Do the recurrent iterations stand for reasoning?

entry.title: Thinking Without More Tokens: Visualizing Recurrent Depth

link.title: Thinking Without More Tokens: Visualizing Recurrent Depth

entry.content:
The core idea

How can we improve a language model’s ability to solve difficult problems without simply making it bigger or asking it to generate more reasoning steps?

Geiping et al. (2025) explore a third scaling approach: recurrent depth. Instead of adding distinct Transformer layers or generating a longer verbal chain of thought, the model repeatedly updates its hidden state using the same four-layer recurrent core. A two-layer prelude processes the input, and a two-layer coda produces next-token probabilities after the recurrent computation.

The authors show that repeating this process can improve the model’s performance on reasoning tasks.

Interactive visualization

The visualization compares three approaches: increasing model size, generating more reasoning tokens, and repeating the same layers internally.

Select an approach, move the slider, and see what changes.

01 / THE MECHANISM

One block. Many passes.

The input is processed once, the recurrent core is reused, and the final state is decoded.

8
11632
Drag to explore.
36
Effective layer applications
8
Distinct Transformer layers
3.5B
Stored model parameters
0
Intermediate reasoning tokens
Shared weights, not independent layers. More passes increase computational depth without increasing stored parameters.
The three modes illustrate different scaling mechanisms, not equal-compute or equal-accuracy comparisons. Parameter and token modes are schematic; the recurrent mode uses the paper's (2, 4, 2) architecture.

What to explore

  1. Scale parameters: Add more independently learned layers.
  2. Scale output tokens: Generate more intermediate reasoning steps.
  3. This paper: Repeat the same four-layer block without adding parameters or reasoning tokens.

In the third approach, 32 repetitions produce an effective depth of 132 layer applications, while the model still has only eight distinct Transformer layers.

The takeaway

A model can do more internal processing without becoming larger or producing more text.

The paper shows that this approach can significantly improve reasoning performance, especially on challenging tasks. Recurrent depth offers a promising new way to make language models better at reasoning by allowing them to think longer before producing an answer.
entry.summary: An interactive comparison of three approaches to improving language model reasoning.

entry.title: A better Figure
entry.content:
The original

Figure 5 of Geiping et al.’s Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach compares three training runs of the 3.5B recurrent-depth model: two failed attempts (“Bad Run 1” and “Bad Run 2”) and the final run (“Main”). It has three plots side by side:

  • Left: training loss.
  • Middle: the correlation of hidden states across the tokens of a sequence. A value of 1.0 means every token has the same hidden state, so the representation has collapsed.
  • Right: validation perplexity, measured at 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 test-time recurrences.

The point of the figure is in the text of the paper, not in the figure itself:

  • Bad Run 1 collapses right away and stalls.
  • Bad Run 2 recovers from the collapse, but learns to ignore the recurrent state, so more recurrences don’t help.
  • The Main run never collapses and keeps improving with more recurrences.

The right plot is the hardest to read. It has 3 runs × 6 recurrence depths = 18 lines, and the depths are told apart only by line style. Because the lines of the failed runs lie on top of each other, the reader has to trust the caption that they overlap.

The redesign

(a) Training loss. (b) Hidden-state correlation; the bold line is a 15-point moving average of the raw curve (faint). (c) Validation perplexity for 1 to 64 recurrences; thick coloured line = 1 recurrence, thin dark lines = 4 to 64.

A scalable version is also available: open the SVG.

The right plot is now three small plots, one per run, and run names are written next to the curves instead of in a legend. In each small plot the 1-recurrence line is thick and the 4 to 64 recurrence lines are thin, dark, and drawn on top of it.

What changed and why

  • One panel per run in the right plot. This is the important change. When the thin lines sit exactly on the thick one, you can see that extra recurrences do nothing. This is the case for both failed runs. In the Main run the lines split: at the end of training 1 recurrence gives a perplexity of about 89 and 16 recurrences give about 7.7, roughly 11× lower. From 8 recurrences on the curves are nearly identical.
  • Direct labels instead of a legend. Each run keeps the same colour in all three plots, and its name is written next to its curve.
  • A dashed ρ = 1 line in the hidden-state plot. It marks total collapse. Bad Run 1 sits on it for its whole life. Bad Run 2 stays on it for about 160 steps and then drops.
  • Smoothing in the hidden-state plot. The raw curves are very noisy, so the bold line is a 15-point moving average and the faint line is the raw data. The original does not smooth this plot. The raw curve also shows a short spike to about 0.89 around step 8 in the Main run, which the average flattens out.
  • Smaller changes. Plain tick labels (10, 100, 1000) instead of exponents on the y-axes, a colourblind-safe palette, and almost no text on the plot itself.

The important change is the first one. The original makes the reader work out from 18 lines that the failed runs gain nothing from recurrence, while the redesign shows it at a glance.

Caveats

  • The data was read from the vector graphics in the paper’s PDF (calibrated against the axis ticks), not re-run. It is as accurate as what the paper shows.
  • The curves end at about step 7,300, although the original caption says the plot covers the first 10,000 steps.
  • In the original, Bad Run 1’s correlation is a flat line at 1.0, and it is redrawn that way.

Code and extracted data: fig5_redo.py, fig5_data.json.
entry.summary: What the new figure makes obvious that the old one didn't.
